1What You Will Learn

  • Explain why containers are used and how they differ from virtual machines
  • Describe images, layers, registries, tags and digests
  • State what the OCI standards and the container runtime stack do
  • Choose the right image pull policy

2Why containers, containers versus virtual machines, what the exam asks

Running case

Harbor Books Packs the Storefront

  • The developer has the storefront as code, plus a list of the libraries it needs
  • The team wants it to run the same way on a laptop, in testing and in the cluster
  • Today the shop is deployed by copying files to servers, and every server is slightly different
  • In this module the storefront becomes a container image

Why Containers: Portable, Dense, Consistent

  • A container packages an app with the files it needs, so it behaves the same wherever it runs
  • Containers decouple the app from the host infrastructure
  • A virtual machine is a whole operating system with its own kernel
  • A container is an isolated process that shares the host's kernel, so more apps fit on less infrastructure

Exam tip

A container is an isolated process, not a small virtual machine.

What the Exam Asks: Containers

  • Container or VM: containers share the host's kernel; a virtual machine brings its own
  • Image or container: the image is the template; the container is a running instance
  • Tag or digest: tags can move; a digest never changes
  • Pull policy: latest or no tag means Always; a version tag means IfNotPresent
  • Docker or CRI: Kubernetes needs a CRI runtime; dockershim was removed in v1.24
  • OCI: the image, runtime and distribution specifications
Exam tip

When a question mixes these terms, decide first which layer it is about: package, standard or runtime.

3Image versus container, layers, registries, tags, digests, pull policy, Dockerfile and multi-stage builds

From Image to Running Container

  • A container image is a ready-to-run package: the code, the runtime it needs and its libraries
  • A container is a running instance of an image; one image can start many containers
  • The life cycle is build, ship, run: build the image, push it to a registry, pull and run it on a node
  • Images are immutable: a change means a new image

Exam tip

The image is the template; the container is what runs.

Image Layers

  • An image is built from layers; each layer is a set of file system changes
  • You start from a base image and add layers for libraries and your own code
  • Because images are immutable, a change adds a layer on top
  • A node downloads only the layers it does not already have

Exam tip

Layers make images efficient: shared layers are stored and pulled once.

Registries, Tags and Digests

Part of the name Example What it means
Registry registry.harborbooks.example where the image is stored; if you leave it out, Kubernetes assumes the Docker public registry
Name storefront the image itself
Tag :1.4 a label for a version; it can be moved to another image; no tag means latest
Digest @sha256:... a hash of the image content; it never changes
  • A tag can be moved; a digest identifies one exact image
  • To run exactly the same image everywhere, reference it by digest
Exam tip

Tags move, digests do not.

Image Pull Policy

imagePullPolicy What the kubelet does
IfNotPresent pulls the image only if it is not already on the node
Always asks the runtime to pull every time a container starts; layers already cached are reused
Never does not pull; the container fails to start if the image is missing
  • If you leave the policy out and use the tag latest, or no tag, it becomes Always
  • If you leave it out and use a version tag or a digest, it becomes IfNotPresent
Exam tip

latest or no tag means Always; a version tag means IfNotPresent.

Dockerfile and Multi-Stage Builds Beyond the curriculum

  • A Dockerfile is a text file of instructions for building an image
  • A multi-stage build uses several FROM lines; each one starts a new stage
  • Build the app in one stage, then copy only the result into the final stage with COPY --from
  • Everything you do not copy is left behind, so the final image is smaller

Build in one stage, ship in another

FROM golang:1.22 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN go build -o /bin/storefront .

FROM alpine:3.20
COPY --from=build /bin/storefront /bin/storefront
CMD ["/bin/storefront"]
Exam tip

Multi-stage builds keep build tools out of the final image.

4The OCI standards

OCI: The Open Standards Archived topic

  • The Open Container Initiative (OCI) develops open standards for containers
  • Image specification: the format of an image
  • Runtime specification: how to run a container from an unpacked filesystem bundle
  • Distribution specification: the API protocol for distributing content through registries
  • runc runs containers according to the OCI specification

Exam tip

OCI means image, runtime and distribution.

5Namespaces and cgroups, the runtime stack, CRI, containerd, CRI-O, runc, dockershim

What a Container Is Made Of: Namespaces and cgroups Beyond the curriculum

  • A container is a process on the host's kernel, isolated and limited by Linux features
  • Namespaces give a process its own isolated view of a system resource
  • Control groups (cgroups) put processes in groups whose resource use can be limited and monitored
  • The kubelet and the runtime use cgroups to enforce CPU and memory requests and limits

Exam tip

Namespaces isolate and cgroups limit; a Linux namespace is not a Kubernetes namespace.

The Runtime Stack: CRI, containerd, CRI-O, runc Beyond the curriculum Old wording

  • The kubelet talks to a runtime through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI)
  • containerd and CRI-O are runtimes that implement the CRI
  • A low-level runtime such as runc creates the container
  • dockershim, the built-in bridge to Docker Engine, was removed in v1.24; Docker-built images still run

Exam tip

Kubernetes needs a CRI runtime such as containerd or CRI-O; dockershim is gone.

6Exam Q&A

6.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer)

S1Which statement correctly compares containers with virtual machines?

  • AEach container runs its own operating system kernel, as a virtual machine does
  • BContainers share the host's kernel, so they are lighter than virtual machines
  • CContainers need a hypervisor to run, while virtual machines do not need one
  • DContainers cannot be isolated from one another, but virtual machines can be
Show the answer

Answer: B. Containers are isolated processes that share the host's kernel, which is why more of them fit on the same infrastructure. A virtual machine carries a whole operating system with its own kernel. Containers do not need a hypervisor, and they are isolated from each other.

S2The Harbor Books team tests an image and then wants production to run exactly the same image. How should the Pod refer to it?

  • ABy the tag latest, because latest always points to the build that was tested
  • BBy a version tag, because a tag cannot be moved after it has been pushed
  • CBy the image name only, because a registry keeps just one version of an image
  • DBy its digest, because a digest identifies one exact image and never changes
Show the answer

Answer: D. A digest is a hash of the image content, so it identifies one exact image. Tags, including latest, can be moved to point to a different image, and a registry can hold many versions under one name.

S3A container uses the image storefront:1.4 and the Pod does not set imagePullPolicy. Which policy does Kubernetes apply?

  • AIfNotPresent, because the tag is a version tag and not latest
  • BAlways, because Kubernetes pulls the image again at each container start
  • CNever, because versioned tags are expected to be on the node already
  • DAlways, because a digest is needed to cache an image on a node
Show the answer

Answer: A. When the policy is left out, a version tag gives IfNotPresent, and so does a digest. Only latest, or no tag at all, gives Always. Never is used only when it is set explicitly.

S4The Harbor Books team pushes a rebuilt storefront image as storefront:1.5. A node already runs storefront:1.4, and only the top layer differs. What does the node download?

  • AThe whole image again, because images cannot be partly cached on a node
  • BNothing, because the node already has an image with the storefront name
  • COnly the layers that the node does not already have in its cache
  • DOnly the first layer, because all later layers are read from the registry
Show the answer

Answer: C. Images are stacks of layers, and the runtime downloads only the layers that are not already cached. Tag 1.5 is a different reference from 1.4, so a pull is needed, but the shared layers are reused.

S5Which OCI specification defines how images are pushed to and pulled from a registry?

  • AThe image specification, which defines the format of an image
  • BThe runtime specification, which defines how a container is run
  • CThe Pod specification, which defines containers in a manifest
  • DThe distribution specification, which defines the registry API protocol
Show the answer

Answer: D. The distribution specification defines the API protocol for distributing content. The image specification defines the image format, the runtime specification defines how a bundle is run, and the Pod specification belongs to Kubernetes, not to the OCI.

S6What is the Container Runtime Interface (CRI)?

  • AThe interface that the kubelet uses to talk to a container runtime
  • BThe standard format in which container images are stored in a registry
  • CA kernel feature that groups processes so that their resource use is limited
  • DThe API protocol with which a registry accepts and serves image layers
Show the answer

Answer: A. The CRI is how the kubelet talks to a runtime such as containerd or CRI-O. The image format and the registry protocol are OCI specifications, and grouping processes to limit resources describes cgroups.

S7A team reads that dockershim was removed in v1.24. What does that mean for its cluster?

  • AImages built with Docker have to be rebuilt, because they are not OCI images
  • BDocker Engine is still built into the kubelet, but it is switched off by default
  • CNodes need a runtime that implements the CRI, such as containerd or CRI-O
  • DContainers need a hypervisor to be installed on each worker node
Show the answer

Answer: C. Kubernetes needs a CRI-compatible runtime on each node. Images built with Docker still run on any runtime, the direct Docker Engine integration is gone rather than switched off, and no hypervisor is needed for containers.
